sentences.text: The petitioner in B.A No.1645 of 2025 is the 1 st accused while the petitioner in B.A No. 2545 of 2025 is the 3 rd accused in Crime No.1277 of 2024 of Mala Police Station, Thrissur.
The crime has been registered alleging offences punishable under sections 406, 409, 420, 465, 468 and 471 r/w section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

3. The F.I.R alleges that the 1 st accused, who was the President of the Kuruvilassery Service Co-operative Bank, the 2 nd accused, who was its Secretary and the 3 rd accused, who was the Junior Clerk, had, in furtherance of their common intention, forged a document in the name of a member of the Society and took a loan of Rs.3,00,000/- on 03.12.2011, took another loan of Rs.1.80 2025:KER:39876 Crores in the name of the 1 st accused and his family members on 29.05.2015 without sufficient security and again on 05.11.2019, suppressed an earlier loan taken in the name of one member of the society and obtained another loan that too in favour of the 1 st accused and thereby committed forgery, criminal breach of trust and cheating and caused a loss of Rs.2,97,82,585/- to the Co- operative Bank and the accused thus committed the offences alleged.
The F.I.R was registered at the instance of the Secretary of the Co-operative Bank pursuant to an audit conducted under section 63 of the Kerala Co-operative Societies Act, 1969.

4. Sri. P. Vijaya Bhanu, the learned Senior Counsel, instructed by Sri. Georgie Simon, the learned counsel for the petitioner in B.A No. 1645 of 2025 contended that the F.I.R was filed only in 2024 in respect of allegations regarding incidents that are alleged to have occurred during the period 2011 to 2019.

It was also submitted that the entire prosecution allegations are false and the crime is registered due to political rivalry and further that as per Annexure 2 affidavit executed by Sri.Prathyuman, it is stated that he has no complaint and he himself had taken the loan.
The learned Senior Counsel also submitted that petitioner is willing to abide by any 2025:KER:39876 conditions that may be imposed and therefore custodial interrogation is not necessary.

5. Sri. Arjun Raghavan, the learned counsel for the petitioner in B.A. No. 2545 of 2025 submitted that the said petitioner was not in service on 03.12.2011 and had in fact entered into service with the bank only on 01.04.2013.
It was also submitted that the name of the 3rd accused had not been mentioned anywhere and he is only an employee of the company who has no role in the matter of grant of loan or its disbursement.

6. Sri. K.A. Noushad, the learned Public Prosecutor on the other hand submitted that the allegations against the petitioners include forgery for the purpose of cheating and other serious offences like criminal breach of trust by a banker, cheating and forgery for that purpose.

It was also submitted that considering the nature of allegations, it is necessary to have custodial interrogation of the petitioners for a proper investigation and only then they will be able to unravel the truth of the matter.

7. Adv. K Vinaya, Adv. N. Anand and Adv. P.K. Sajeev, the learned counsel appearing for additional respondents 5 to 7 respectively, also submitted that the F.I.R was filed subsequent to 2025:KER:39876 Annexure R6(a) statutory audit report where the roles of each of the accused were specifically mentioned.

It was also pointed out that in the recent elections, the accused were elected and immediately the defacto complainant was suspended from service for having filed the complaint Dojo Davis vs State Of Kerala on 4 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/54086483/
5 pursuant to the statutory audit, while the 3rd accused who was earlier under suspension was reinstated.

sentences.text: The learned counsel also pointed out that large scale financial misappropriation had taken place in the Society while the 1 st accused was the President and the same property was used as a security for different loans after showing bloated figures as the value of the property.

Further,
out of the total of 18 loans given to the 1st accused and his family members, no security of sufficient value was taken from the said accused and they have made unlawful gains for themselves and loss to the society.
8. I have considered the rival contentions.
9. The 1st accused was the President of the Society for more than 30 years.

He is alleged to have,
with the assistance of the other bank officers, forged documents and created fabricated loan accounts and transferred large amounts to his personal account.
Section 63 of the Co-operative Societies Act, 1969 provides for an 2025:KER:39876 audit of a Co-operative Society.

In the statutory audit conducted in 2024, as evident from Annexure XV produced in B.A. No. 2545 of 2025 and Annexure R5(d) produced in B.A No. 1645 of 2025, the auditors had, after referring to the specific instances of cheating, misappropriation and forgery, directed the registration of a crime and to conduct an investigation either by the Police or by the Vigilance.
The F.I.R has been registered pursuant to the said audit report.
In the audit report, the auditors have identified three instances as indicating the commission of cheating and other offences.

One of the instances referred to therein,
includes the 1 st accused having taken 18 loans in the name of his family members based on insufficient security.
Apart from there being no sufficient security for the loans, the bank has become unable to recover the amount of Rs.2.75 Crores and has caused huge loss to the Society.
10. The 3 rd accused is alleged to have inserted forged signatures of a member of the Bank by name Smt. Remya.

Though it was argued that as the incident alleged is even prior to the third accused joining the Bank, the allegation is baseless, on a perusal of the records, it is seen that the 3 rd accused joined the Bank in 2013 while the offence is alleged to have been committed in 2015.
The offences alleged against the petitioners include forgery for the purpose of cheating and criminal breach of trust by a banker and cheating.
The departmental auditors had specifically referred to the instances which revealed the involvement of the petitioners and even directed registration of a crime.
Taking note of the seriousness of the allegations and also the nature of offences alleged, only a custodial interrogation would be able to reveal the truth of the matter.

12. The contention of the petitioner in B.A. No. 2545 of 2025 that as the allegations can all be investigated based on documents, though impressive at first blush, on a deeper scrutiny, it is noted that the nature of allegations indicates the requirement of investigation not only based on documents but even otherwise.

The common intention of the accused to commit the offences, the fraudulent and dishonest manner in which forged documents were allegedly used and the manner in which the society was allegedly cheated are all matters which could be properly probed into only by custodial interrogation.

sentences.text: Further, in matters where the allegations are serious, it is not proper to grant anticipatory bail as held in Supreme Bhiwandi 2025:KER:39876 Wada Manor Infrastructure Private Limited v State of Maharashtra and Another (2021) 8 SCC 753.

entities.text: Supreme Bhiwandi 2025:KER:39876 Wada Manor Infrastructure Private Limited v State of Maharashtra and Another (2021) 8 SCC 753
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In the said decision, relying upon the decision in Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another [(2020) 5 SCC 1], it was observed that, while considering whether to grant anticipatory bail or not, Courts ought to be generally guided by considerations such as the nature and gravity of the offences, the role attributed to the applicant,
and the facts of the case.

entities.text: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another [(2020) 5 SCC 1]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Further, in the decision in Brijmani Devi v. Pappu Kumar and Another [(2022) 4 SCC 497] it was observed that though liberty of an individual is an invaluable right, at the same time, while considering an application for bail, courts cannot lose sight of the serious nature of accusations against an accused and the facts that have a bearing in the case, particularly when the accusations may not be false, frivolous, or vexatious in nature but are supported by adequate material brought on record so as to enable a court to arrive at a conclusion.

entities.text: Brijmani Devi v. Pappu Kumar and Another [(2022) 4 SCC 497]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 14. In a recent decision in P. Krishna Mohan Reddy vs. State of Andra Pradesh (2025 LiveLaw SC 598) the Supreme Court had observed that custodial interrogation is qualitatively 2025:KER:39876 more elicitation oriented than questioning a suspect who is well ensconced with a favourable order of pre-arrest bail.

entities.text: P. Krishna Mohan Reddy vs. State of Andra Pradesh (2025 LiveLaw SC 598)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was also observed that success in interrogation will elude if the suspected person knows that he is well protected and insulated by a pre- arrest bail order during the time he is interrogated.
In fact, the court went on to hold that insulating a person from arrest would make his interrogation a mere ritual.
15. The aforesaid observations assume significance in the instant case.
The offence under section 409 IPC is punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment for ten years.
When such serious offences are alleged, grant of anticipatory bail is not justified, especially when the statutory auditors had prima facie identified instances of criminal acts.
The allegations also indicate that valuation of property was bloated to secure several loans on the basis of the same security.
Similarly, loans for family members are alleged to have been provided on the basis of the same security.
The manner and nature of commission of these acts could be revealed only through custodial interrogation.

Restricting the investigating agency from indulging in or from carrying out custodial interrogation would only lead to serious prejudice and it 2025:KER:39876 may even turn out to be just a mere ritual.
In view of the nature of allegations and the circumstances arising in the case, this Court is of the view that the petitioners cannot be protected with a pre-arrest bail.
Hence, these bail applications are dismissed.

Sd/-

The offence under section 409 IPC is punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment for ten years.
When such serious offences are alleged, grant of anticipatory bail is not justified, especially when the statutory auditors had prima facie identified instances of criminal acts.
The allegations also indicate that valuation of property was bloated to secure several loans on the basis of the same security.

The F.I.R alleges that the 1 st accused, who was the President of the Kuruvilassery Service Co-operative Bank, the 2 nd accused, who was its Secretary and the 3 rd accused, who was the Junior Clerk, had, in furtherance of their common intention, forged a document in the name of a member of the Society and took a loan of Rs.3,00,000/- on 03.12.2011, took another loan of Rs.1.80 2025:KER:39876 Crores in the name of the 1 st accused and his family members on 29.05.2015 without sufficient security and again on 05.11.2019, suppressed an earlier loan taken in the name of one member of the society and obtained another loan that too in favour of the 1 st accused and thereby committed forgery, criminal breach of trust and cheating and caused a loss of Rs.2,97,82,585/- to the Co- operative Bank and the accused thus committed the offences alleged.
The F.I.R was registered at the instance of the Secretary of the Co-operative Bank pursuant to an audit conducted under section 63 of the Kerala Co-operative Societies Act, 1969.

Further,
out of the total of 18 loans given to the 1st accused and his family members, no security of sufficient value was taken from the said accused and they have made unlawful gains for themselves and loss to the society.
He is alleged to have,
with the assistance of the other bank officers, forged documents and created fabricated loan accounts and transferred large amounts to his personal account.
Section 63 of the Co-operative Societies Act, 1969 provides for an 2025:KER:39876 audit of a Co-operative Society.
Taking note of the seriousness of the allegations and also the nature of offences alleged, only a custodial interrogation would be able to reveal the truth of the matter.
The common intention of the accused to commit the offences, the fraudulent and dishonest manner in which forged documents were allegedly used and the manner in which the society was allegedly cheated are all matters which could be properly probed into only by custodial interrogation.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Further, in matters where the allegations are serious, it is not proper to grant anticipatory bail as held in Supreme Bhiwandi 2025:KER:39876 Wada Manor Infrastructure Private Limited v State of Maharashtra and Another (2021) 8 SCC 753.
14. In a recent decision in P. Krishna Mohan Reddy vs. State of Andra Pradesh (2025 LiveLaw SC 598) the Supreme Court had observed that custodial interrogation is qualitatively 2025:KER:39876 more elicitation oriented than questioning a suspect who is well ensconced with a favourable order of pre-arrest bail.
In view of the nature of allegations and the circumstances arising in the case, this Court is of the view that the petitioners cannot be protected with a pre-arrest bail.
